 Education — Re-envisioning the blueprint for collective progress
  Education is the cornerstone of societal progress, acting as the primary driver of economic growth, poverty 
reduction, and social mobility. Naturally, education remains a cornerstone of the Foundation’s commitment to 
building inclusive and sustainable community. The Foundation’s education initiatives focus on supporting students from underserved communities at different stages of their learning journey - ranging from school education to higher education and preparation for employment. In addition to academic support, the Foundation follows a holistic approach that combines academics with sports, digital learning, life skills, and career preparedness, helping students build confidence, practical abilities, and long-term career readiness.
  During the r eporting period, the Foundation implemented education initiatives across six locations in partnership 
with 31 grassroots and institutional non-governmental organisations. Through 29 education-focused projects and 18 study centres, the Foundation supported 48 schools and four colleges. These initiatives reached  35,107 students, including 19,604 unique beneficiaries. A total investment of INR 724.56 lakh enabled the delivery of impactful, scalable, and sustainable education programmes, strengthening access to quality education in the communities served.

Health — Helping our littlest fighters win their biggest battles
The Foundation’s health initiatives are driven by a strong commitment to providing accessible, affordable, and 
preventive healthcare to underserved communities. The focus is on improving health outcomes by addressing both immediate medical needs and long-term well-being. The Foundation supports preventive care, treatment-based assistance, community outreach programmes, and specialised medical interventions to ensure timely and effective healthcare support for vulnerable populations.
Working closely with credible healthcare institutions and non-governmental organisations, the Foundation 
emphasises early diagnosis, timely treatment, and outreach to communities with limited access to quality healthcare services. Preventive healthcare remains a key priority, helping reduce disease burden and enabling early identification of health conditions. In addition, the Foundation provides support for specialised and high-cost medical procedures, ensuring that financial limitations do not prevent individuals from receiving essential treatment.
Key health interventions during the year included:•
 Cochlear  implant support for children with hearing impairment
• Cardiac surgeries for patients from economically disadvantaged backgrounds
• Support f or essential and critical surgeries across multiple medical specialties
These interventions have played a vital role in saving lives and significantly improving the long-term quality of life for 
beneficiaries.

Report of the DirectorsCommunity Development – Livelihood Project
Wildlife and Heritage conservation — Rooting advancement in our cultural and natural inheritance
As part of its commitment to protecting wildlife and maintaining ecological balance, the Foundation supported 
the use of technology to strengthen conservation efforts and reduce conflict between humans and wildlife. Drone cameras were deployed to track the movement of wild animals and monitor forest areas. These drones were also used for tiger census activities and to observe elephant movement in sensitive corridors. This enabled timely monitoring, better coordination on the ground, and quicker response to potential risks.
These efforts support the forest department in safeguarding wildlife habitats and help create awareness among local 
communities. By providing early alerts and reliable tracking information, the initiatives play an important role in preventing human-wildlife conflict and improving safety for both people and animals.
Alongside wildlife conservation, the Foundation also supported heritage preservation and public education by contributing to 
the upkeep and improvement of museum infrastructure. This included maintenance work and upgrades to essential facilities, enabling effective use of audio guide systems for visitors.
Infrastructure support was also extended to Shivsrushti, a historic theme park in Pune, where digital display screens were 
installed to enhance storytelling and provide visitors with a more engaging and educational experience through immersive visual content.
In line with its CSR commitment to wildlife care, the Foundation also supported the operations of an aviary providing medical 
treatment to injured and rescued birds. During the year, 673 birds across six species received care, of which 509 were successfully rehabilitated and released back into their natural habitats. These efforts contributed meaningfully to biodiversity conservation and the restoration of local ecosystems.

Report of the DirectorsEmployee Engagement
At the Foundation, employee engagement is at the heart of its CSR efforts, reflecting a culture where employees 
voluntarily contribute their time, skills, and care to support communities. Through well-structured volunteering opportunities across education, health, environment, and community development, employees are encouraged to participate actively and create meaningful social impact.
During the year, employee volunteering continued to see strong participation. A total of 5,841 employees contributed 
11,683 hours across 70 initiatives. Overall, 299 volunteering activities were conducted across 15 locations, reflecting broad participation and geographic reach.
Volunteering programmes were designed to be inclusive and flexible, enabling employees across roles and locations 
to participate alongside their regular work commitments. On average, each volunteer contributed close to two hours, reflecting consistent and high quality engagement. Locations such as Pune, Nagpur, Hyderabad, and Goa recorded particularly strong participation, supported by effective local coordination and employee-led initiatives.
In addition to volunteering, employees actively supported the Foundation through donation drives, further 
strengthening the culture of giving. Employee contributions during the year amounted to INR 47.12 lakh, supplemented by INR 34.79 lakh from other sources. Together, these contributions played an important role in strengthening the Foundation’s social programmes and extending their reach.

Report of the DirectorsAnnexure E - Energy Conservation and Technology Absorption: Key Initiatives 
The Company has achieved carbon neutrality for Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions for three consecutive years (FY 24, FY 
25 and FY 26), as per ISO 14068-1:2023, reflecting its continued focus on climate action and responsible operations.
Carbon neutrality has been sustained through a combination of energy efficiency improvements, increased renewable 
energy adoption, and implementation of climate-conscious policies across operations and the value chain. The Company continues to align its approach with evolving global and national sustainability standards, with a focus on enhancing long-term environmental resilience.
The Company continues to enhance energy efficiency across its operations through a combination of green building 
design, technology adoption, and operational optimisation.
Key energy initiatives include:Deployment of advanced HVAC solutions:•
  Replacement of legacy systems with energy-efficient inverter-based systems using eco-friendly refrigerants (R32 / 
R410A)
•  Implemen tation of demand-controlled ventilation systems to optimise energy use and enhance indoor air quality, 
reducing treated fresh air AHU power consumption
• Deploymen t of cold aisle containment in data centres to reduce HVAC energy load
• Installation of HVLS fans in large spaces to enhance comfort and reduce dependence on air conditioning
• Introduction of mist cooling systems in outdoor cafeterias and common areas
• Evaluation and adoption of adiabatic cooling solutions for 24×7 data centre and server room operations
• Automation of AHU for energy saving and human comfort
Lighting Optimisation Initiatives•
 Comple te transition to LED-based lighting infrastructure
•  Adoption of  automated, sensor-driven lighting systems, including occupancy and motion sensors, for efficient energy 
utilisation
Integrated Energy Management and Operational Efficiency•
 Enabled cen tralised monitoring through an integrated Building Management System (BMS)
•  Implemen ted dynamic optimisation of air conditioning operations, based on occupancy, seasonal variations and work 
schedules
•  Incorpor ated energy-efficient design features such as double wall construction, low-E glazing, double-glazed units 
(DGUs), underdeck insulation, and optimised daylight utilisation
• Deploy ed power quality systems (ASVG, AHF, APFC) to maintain near-unity power factor and control harmonics
• Upgr aded to high-efficiency modular UPS systems to minimise transmission and operational losses
•  Transitioned to a 100% laptop-based computing environment to reduce energy demand and associated HVAC load
•  Optimised oper ations through regulated scheduling of utilities including lifts, lighting, ventilation, water coolers, and 
vending machines during non-operating hours
•  Installed Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs) in AHUs and fresh air systems for enhanced control and energy optimisation
•  Implemen ted dynamic optimisation of air conditioning operations, based on occupancy, seasonal variations and work 
schedules

Report on Corporate Governance
Company’s beliefs on Corporate Governance
“Corporate governance is concerned with holding the balance between economic and social goals and aligning the 
interests of individuals, corporations and society. ”
 - Sir Adrian Cadbury
Redefining Stakeholders for a Sustainable Future
Traditionally, the stakeholders of a public limited company have been defined in legal terms, comprising shareholders, 
debenture-holders, deposit-holders, and other security holders. While such a definition remains relevant, the Company believes that in the context of a modern and evolving business environment, the scope of stakeholders must extend far beyond statutory classifications.
 At Persistent, we recognise that long-term value creation is intrinsically linked with the interests of all those 
who contribute to, and are impacted by, our operations. Accordingly, our approach to stakeholder engagement encompasses not only our investors, but also our employees and their families, customers, business partners, vendors, regulators, and the communities and ecosystems within which we operate.
 In line with this philosoph y, the Board of Directors has affirmed a broader and more inclusive definition of 
stakeholders. This approach aligns with the Company’s sustainability vision and reinforces its commitment to creating shared and enduring value for all stakeholder groups.
Our Commitment to Responsible Governance
Corporate Governance is a fundamental cornerstone of our operations and is anchored in the principles of trust, 
transparency, and accountability. Our governance framework is designed to balance the interests of a diverse stakeholder base while enabling robust and ethical decision-making that supports sustainable business growth.
 Integrity, inclusivity, and sustainability are fundamental to the Company’s corporate culture. Through continuous 
enhancement of governance practices, we strive to uphold the highest standards of accountability while contributing positively to the broader economic, social, and environmental ecosystem.
 This sec tion presents an overview of how the Company engages with stakeholders, integrates Environmental, Social, 
and Governance (ESG) considerations into strategy, and seeks to deliver long-term sustainable value. 
1. Emplo yees and their Families 
  The Compan y’s continued success is driven by the expertise, commitment, and dedication of employees. 
Senior employees play a critical role in shaping the Company’s strategic direction and overseeing operations. 
Recognising the vital support extended by employees’ families, the Company remains committed to safeguarding their overall well-being.
2.
 Clients
   The Compan y provides services to its clients because of which we earn our revenue. Their satisfaction and delight 
are important focus areas of the Company’s operations. Our clients are keen that we succeed and continue to deliver on our promises and hence, they are also vested in our success.
3.
 Partners
  The Compan y collaborates with its partners to deliver value to its clients. These relationships are built on mutual 
trust and shared objectives. The Company believes that the strength and success of its partnerships are integral to its own growth and endeavours to support the long-term success of its partners.
4.
 Suppliers 
  The Compan y relies on a network of suppliers for various goods and services essential to its operations. Operational 
efficiency is closely linked to the quality and reliability of these contributions. The Company is committed to maintaining fair and sustainable relationships with its suppliers and supporting their long-term growth.

5. Shareowners/Investors 
  Shareowners are the owners of the Company and are the traditional stakeholders in the Company. They have 
invested in the Company, and we believe it is our responsibility to deliver fair returns to our shareowners.
6. Environment
  It is a constant endeavour of the Company to conserve and preserve the environment. Over the years, the Company has focused on sustainable business practices encompassing economic, environmental, and social imperatives. The Company also works through Persistent Foundation and Persistent India Foundation, to support projects in the areas of environmental sustainability and ecological balance. 
  T o maintain and strengthen relationships with its stakeholders, the Company has established structured 
mechanisms and governance processes. The Company remains aligned with global sustainability goals and continues to monitor and enhance its performance against ESG metrics.
  Stakeholder relationships are managed through clearly defined roles and responsibilities across the organisation. The Board of Directors and leadership teams periodically review these activities to ensure adherence to the highest standards of governance.
  The Nomina tion and Remuneration Committee (‘NRC’) oversees matters relating to employees, while the Stakeholders’ 
Relationship and ESG Committee (‘SRC’) is entrusted with addressing the interests of investors, shareholders, and other security holders in accordance with applicable laws. The Company has also brought ESG oversight within the purview of the SRC to ensure focused Board-level attention to sustainability initiatives.
  To enable a coordinated approach to stakeholder engagement, the SRC receives inputs from management and other 
relevant committees and prepares an annual report for submission to the Board. This report forms an integral part of the Company’s disclosures.
  The Compan y believes that strong Corporate Governance practices are essential for enhancing long-term stakeholder 
value. Continuous improvement in governance standards remains a key priority, enabling the Company to build trust, strengthen resilience, and support sustainable growth.
  This Report on Corporate Governance reflects the Company’s ongoing commitment to adhering to governance principles in both letter and spirit, while striving to maintain the highest standards of integrity and transparency.

  i. T o manage and direct the business and affairs of the Company
  ii.  T o manage, subject to the Articles of Association of the Company, its affairs, including planning its 
composition, selecting its Chairman, appointing Committees, establishing the terms of reference and duties

  iii.  T o act honestly and in good faith in the best interests and objects of the Company, its employees, its 
shareholders including minority shareholders, the community, and for the protection of the environment 
  iv .   T o ensure that the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) and the Management operate in the best long-term 
interests of the Company  and all stakeholders and to monitor the CEO’s performance and as and when appropriate, make necessary changes
  v .   T o ensure that the succession planning is undertaken for the Chief Executives of the Company, including the 
Chief Executive Officer (CEO)
  vi To plan, monitor and approve the remuneration payable to Key Managerial Personnel of the Company
  vii.  T o exercise due care, diligence, and skill that a reasonably prudent person would exercise in comparable 
circumstances and shall also exercise independent judgment
  viii.  T o participate directly or through its committees, in defining, developing and approving the mission of the

  i x.   T o ensure congruence between shareholders’ expectations, the Company’s goals, objectives, and management 
performance
  x .   T o monitor the Company’s progress towards its goals and to revise and alter its direction in light of changing 
circumstances 
  xi.  T o approve and monitor compliance with all significant policies and procedures by which the Company is 
operated

 e. Boar d Meetings and Deliberations
   The Compan y Secretary, in consultation with the Chairman of the Board of Directors and the Chairpersons 
of the respective Board Committees, prepares the agenda and supporting documents for discussion at each Board / Committee meeting, respectively. Members of the Board or Committees may suggest items to be included in the agenda. In addition, they have the right to bring matters for discussion at the meeting with the permission of the Chairpersons.
   Information and data that are important for the Board to understand the business of the Company and current 
affairs are tabled for discussion at the meeting. The agenda is circulated in writing to the members of the Board at least seven calendar days before the meeting in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 (the ‘Act’) and the Secretarial Standard – 1 (‘SS-1’) issued by the Institute of Company Secretaries of India.

 f. Performance Evaluation of the Board, its Committees and Individual Directors
   The Compan y conducted the annual performance evaluation of the Board, the Chairman, its various 
Committees and the Directors individually, including the Independent Directors. In accordance with the 
provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, the performance evaluation was undertaken with the assistance of an external management consultant specialising in Board evaluations.
   The e valuation was carried out through a structured process covering various aspects of the Board’s 
functioning, including composition and structure, effectiveness of Board processes, quality and timeliness of information flow, engagement and participation in deliberations, strategic oversight, governance effectiveness, risk management and compliance, along with qualitative inputs and perspectives on the future direction of the Board and the Company. The performance of the Board was assessed through inputs obtained from all Directors and select senior management executives. 
   The e valuation process also covered the performance of the Board Committees against the requirements of 
their respective charters and the effectiveness in discharging their responsibilities. The external consultant conducted one-on-one interactions with each Board Member to obtain detailed feedback.
   The Boar d reviewed and discussed the outcomes of the evaluation in an executive session and noted that 
the Board, its Committees and the Directors, including the Independent Directors, continued to function effectively and demonstrated a high level of engagement, objectivity and preparedness in their roles. The evaluation process also enabled identification of areas for continuous improvement further improving overall Board effectiveness. The Board has taken note of these inputs and will address them as part of its ongoing governance and development initiatives.
   The e valuation for FY 2025-26 was conducted in March and April 2026. The findings of the evaluation were 
presented at the meetings of the Nomination and Remuneration Committee and the Board of Directors held in April 2026.

 Those Char ged with Governance (TCWG) Committee
  Your Company has constituted a ‘Those Charged with Governance (TCWG) Committee’ pursuant to the National 
Financial Reporting Authority (‘NFRA’) Circular dated January 7, 2026, with the framework becoming effective from April 1, 2026. TCWG comprises the Board of Directors, with the Audit Committee acting as a delegated sub-group, along with key executives including the Chairman and Managing Director, Executive Directors (CEO and CFO), and the Company Secretary. TCWG is responsible for overseeing strategic direction, financial reporting, internal controls, audit matters, and ensuring appropriate escalation of significant issues such as fraud, going concern risks, and regulatory non-compliance to the Board. The Company has designated nodal persons from both sides to facilitate communication as follows:
Company’s Side Statutory Auditor’s Side

Disclosures
Code of Conduct
 Pursuant to the requirements of Regulation 17(5)(a) of Listing Regulations, the Company obtains the affirmation of compliance 
of the Code of Conduct from its Directors and Senior Management on a yearly basis since Financial Year 2005-06. 
Furthermore, the Code of Conduct applies to all the Company employees and its subsidiaries.
 The Code of  Conduct is an annual declaration that helps remind all employees and stakeholders the importance of maintaining 
the highest standards of ethical business conduct for the Company. In terms of the Code of Conduct, Directors and Employees must act within the guidelines of the authority conferred upon them and with a duty to make and enact informed decisions and policies in the best interests of the Company and its shareholders and stakeholders.
Further, Directors and Employees must ensure that they do not derive any undue personal benefit due to their position in the 
Company and from the access they have to certain confidential information coming to their knowledge.
 It has been a ffirmed by the Board of Directors that the Code of Conduct has been complied with by all the Board members and 
all the Employees and a declaration to this effect forms part of this Report. The Code of Conduct is uploaded on the website of the Company at Code of Conduct for Directors and Employees | Persistent Systems 
In addition to the annual Code of Conduct, the Board has also established a robust Code of Conduct on Prevention of Insider 
Trading in terms of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. The Company has a zero tolerance policy towards insider trading, corruption, bribery, and money laundering.
Familiarisation Program for the Board of DirectorsPursuant to the requirements of Regulation 25(7) of Listing Regulations, the Company conducts the Familiarisation Program for 
Independent Directors as well as other Directors on the Board about their roles, rights, responsibilities in the Company, nature of the industry in which the Company operates, business model of the Company, etc., through various initiatives. The Company also shares the organogram and important organisational changes on a regular basis. A few initiatives under familiarisation program are elaborated at https://www.persistent.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Familiarization-Programme-2025-26.pdf
Board deliberations on strategy planningAs part of our annual strategy planning process, the Company organises sessions for the Board Members and Senior Executives 
to deliberate on various topics related to technological overview, global scenario for the IT industry, sales strategy, market research, risk overview, succession planning and strategic programs required to achieve the Company’s long-term objectives.
 The Compan y organises periodic planning meetings called the ‘Huddle’, which is attended by all the senior sales and delivery 
leaders of the Organisation. Board Members participate in the Huddle to get a first-hand view of the strategy planning and implementation process and guide the leadership by offering their expertise.
 This serv es a dual purpose of providing a platform for Board Members to bring their expertise to the projects, while also 
providing an opportunity for them to understand detailed aspects of execution and challenges relating to the business of  
the Company.
Whistleblower PolicyThe Board of Directors of the Company has a Whistleblower Policy for employees and non-employee stakeholders in India and 
all global locations. The employees are encouraged to report to the Whistleblower Administrator if they observe any fraudulent financial or other information or conduct that results in instances of unethical behaviour, or actual or suspected violations of the Company’s Code of Conduct and the Ethics Policy.
 The employ ees are actively encouraged to reach out to the Whistleblower Administrator if they observe any fraudulent activity, 
questionable financial practices, or conduct that appears unethical, or if they suspect violations of the Company’s Code of Conduct or Ethics Policy. Beginning FY 2025-26, the Head of the Ethics Committee serves as the Whistleblower Administrator, personally overseeing the investigation process from the initial complaint through to its resolution. All findings and outcomes are subsequently reported to the Chairperson of the Audit Committee. Importantly, complainants are permitted to submit their concerns in any local language, ensuring accessibility for all.
The Company has also taken proactive initiatives to train employees and raise awareness about the Vigil Mechanism, reinforcing 
a culture of transparency and ethical conduct. These initiatives, along with the policy itself, provide robust safeguards to protect employees from any form of victimisation when they report issues to the Whistleblower Administrator.

including the “Other Method” prescribed under Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with Rule 10AB of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, and the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines. Based on its economic analysis, PwC has reported that both transactions can be considered to be in accordance with the arm’s length standard required under the Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations.

Data Protection InitiativesInformation SecurityYour Company maintains a mature Information Security Management System with Policies, Processes and Controls to  
minimise the Cyber Security Risks. The governance and management of security compliance and risk is reviewed periodically. 
Your Company’s development centres are certified under ISO 27001, ISO 27017, ISO 27018, ISO 27701, ISO 22301, ISO 42001 and SOC 2 Type II.
 Your Company is focused on cyber resilience and provides all the necessary budgets needed to build a robust cyber resilience. 
Your Company’s Global IT and Information Security team has taken a holistic and comprehensive approach, including the customer-specific security requirements where applicable, to address the need to secure the employees’ laptops, the corporate network, and confidential data including Personal data against inadvertent and malicious attacks. Your Company’s cloud first strategy is enabled by cloud security measures spanning access management, cloud data security, ensuring privacy in the cloud, safeguarding cloud workloads, effective monitoring and incident management of the cloud aligned to business-relevant outcomes. Throughout the year, your company has made substantial efforts to enhance security & data privacy awareness and training across the organisation. Cloud security, Privilege Access Management, Data Loss Prevention, and Supplier Security

& Privacy management were prioritised to protect company infrastructure, safeguard data and maintain the integrity and 
confidentiality throughout the supply chain and improve overall security posture of your company.
 Specific s teps include allocation of secure laptops to every employee, installation of disk encryption, next generation antivirus 
solution, enhanced data leakage prevention solutions, implementation of Multi Factor Authentication, Secure and governed internet access, and Zero Trust Model to ensure cyber resiliency. The emailing solution is equipped with advance anti-phishing functionality ensuring a secure channel of communication through email.
 Your Company has implemented a robust disaster recovery process with a well-articulated cyber resilience playbook. The 
periodic Disaster Recovery drills ensure availability of the critical services and the ability to recover business operations as per the defined process. Your Company has a steadfast focus on spreading information security & data privacy awareness through mandatory awareness trainings at joining followed by periodic refresher sessions and usage of enterprise-wide communication and collaboration platforms to keep users updated on evolving cybersecurity and privacy risks. The training effectiveness is validated through periodic phishing simulations.

Details of Non-compliance
During the year under review, an application for compounding of an offence under Section 96 of the Companies 
Act, 2013 was filed with the Regional Director, Mumbai in respect of M/s. Capiot Software Private Limited, a Wholly Owned subsidiary Company which was merged with your Company. The said violation pertained to non-compliance with the provisions relating to the holding of the Annual General Meeting within the prescribed timelines. The application was duly considered by the Regional Director, Mumbai, and the offence has been compounded upon payment of the requisite compounding fee as determined under the Act. The Company has taken note of the matter and has instituted necessary measures to further strengthen its compliance framework and ensure adherence to statutory timelines on a continual basis.
The aforesaid compounding does not have any material impact on the financial statements, operations, or other 
business activities of the Listed Company. The management continues to maintain robust compliance systems and periodic monitoring mechanisms to mitigate such instances going forward.
 Ther e were no non-compliances by the Company, no penalties and strictures were imposed on the Company by 
Stock Exchanges, SEBI or any statutory authority, on any matter related to the capital markets, during the year April 1, 2025, to March 31, 2026.

22. Nomina tion in Respect of Shares
   Section 72 of the Act provides facility for making nominations by Members in respect of their holding of shares. 
Such nomination greatly facilitates transmission of shares from the deceased Member to his / her nominee without being required to go through the process of obtaining Succession Certificates / Probate of the Will, etc. It would, therefore, be in the best interest of the Members holding shares as a sole holder to make such nomination.
  Member s holding shares in physical mode are advised to submit form SH-13 which is available for download at 
https://www.persistent.com/investors/%20investors-communication/notice-to-physical-shareholders/ to the Registrar and Share Transfer Agent of the Company for making the nomination. Members holding shares in demat form are advised to contact their DP for making the nominations. Members are further requested to quote their E-mail IDs, Telephone / Fax numbers for prompt reply to their communication.

1. Climate 
Strategy (Transition & Physical Risks and Emission & Energy Management)R / O Risk:
Climate change presents 
material risks to the Company through physical impacts, including disruption to data centres and office operations from extreme weather events, increased energy costs and supply chain interruptions. In addition, regulatory and transition risks—such as evolving climate regulations, carbon pricing mechanisms, and client sustainability mandates—may increase compliance costs, expose the Company to financial penalties, and affect operational continuity and competitiveness. Together, physical and transition risks have the potential to influence costs, service delivery and long-term business resilience.
Opportunity:A proactive climate strategy 
focused on decarbonising operations, improving energy efficiency and investing in low carbon technologies presents a significant growth and resilience opportunity. Advancing climate action can reduce operating costs, mitigate regulatory and energy price risks and strengthen the Company’s competitive positioning. In parallel, it enables the development of green IT and digital sustainability solutions, supports compliance with client climate expectations and attracts sustainability driven customers, thereby creating long-term value and market differentiation.Strong commitment and action-oriented short-, medium- and long-term plan to reducing our carbon footprint through renewable energy adoption and energy efficiency measures and accounting of GHG emissions across Scope 1, 2, and 3.
In line with these commitments, 
we achieved carbon neutrality for Scope 1 and 2 emissions for three consecutive years starting FY 2023-24, FY 2024-25, & FY 2025-26.
We commit to reach Net-Zero 
greenhouse gas emissions across the value chain by 2050. Our net-zero strategy drives innovation in clean technologies and energy efficiency, ensuring long-term climate resilience.

2. Details on Sustainable Sourcing
a.  Does the entity  have procedures in place for sustainable sourcing? 
Yes. Persistent Systems Limited has an end -to-end sustainable sourcing process, covering vendor screening, 
contract onboarding and ongoing supplier monitoring. Sustainability considerations are embedded into 
procurement through green procurement practices, assessment of environmental and social impacts prior to contract award, and integration of environmental and social clauses in supplier contracts. Suppliers are required to comply with the Company’s Vendor Code of Conduct, which outlines expectations on ethical business conduct, environmental protection, labour standards, health and safety and human rights. Persistent encourages suppliers to adopt responsible sourcing, waste reduction and energy
-efficient operational 
practices.
   In addition, P ersistent undertakes regular supplier ESG engagement and assessments, including initiatives 
aligned with SEBI BRSR Core requirements, to build ESG awareness and promote responsible practices across the value chain. These assessments and capacity
-building initiatives support the identification and management 
of sustainability -related risks. The Company also emphasises inclusive procurement by actively engaging local 
suppliers, including MSMEs, thereby supporting local economic development while strengthening supply  chain resilience. Refer Vendor Code of Conduct
b.
 If yes, what percentage of inputs were sourced sustainably?  
  Sustainable sourcing is integrated into procurement processes, with a strong focus on eco-certified materials. 
Over the past year, the AR PG facility in Pune underwent a complete refurbishment and about 85% of the furniture purchased was eco-certified, demonstrating consistently high adoption. The Company continues to work with suppliers to further increase eco-certified sourcing.

3.  Accessibility of workplaces 
Are the premises / offices of the entity accessible to differently abled employees and workers, as per the requirements of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016? If not, whether any steps are being taken by the entity in this regard. 
 Yes, Persistent Systems has a strong emphasis on accessibility and inclusion, with a focus on creating enablement 
friendly workplaces for persons with disabilities. The Company is committed to providing an inclusive, barrier free work environment and endeavours to ensure that its offices and premises are accessible in line with the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016, and the Harmonised Guidelines issued thereunder.
  Persistent offices are designed to accommodate the needs of persons with disabilities and include features such 
as accessible parking spaces, ramps at entry points, elevators, appropriate signage, disabled friendly restrooms, and height adjustable workstations, including provisions to support wheelchair users. Across all leased facilities, the Company ensures that accessibility requirements for persons with disabilities are duly addressed. In the digital environment, Persistent follows recognised accessibility standards and adheres to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.0) to enhance accessibility of internal digital platforms. Where required, assistive technologies and reasonable accommodations are provided to support employees with specific needs. The Company conducts periodic reviews and audits of its facilities and undertakes necessary infrastructure upgrades on a continuous basis to further strengthen accessibility and inclusion, ensuring that individuals of all abilities can seamlessly access and engage with both physical and digital work environments. All our India Owned facilities including leased facilities are accessible to Persons with Disabilities.

b. 
 Wha t are the processes used to identify work-related hazards and assess risks on a routine and non-routine 
basis by the entity?
   Persistent’s Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) programmes are designed to proactively identify, assess 
and mitigate risks that could impact employee health, safety and well-being across all locations. In line with ISO 45001:2018 principles, the company follows a structured Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA) approach covering all routine and non-routine activities within office premises and other operational environments.
  As a services-led or ganisation, our OHS risk landscape primarily includes ergonomics-related risks, psychosocial 
factors, utilities and infrastructure safety, biological hazards, unsafe conditions, employee commute safety and others. Risks are systematically assessed using a comprehensive Risk Identification and Hazard Assessment Matrix that evaluates hazards based on severity, likelihood and potential impact. This assessment framework covers unsafe acts, unsafe conditions, new or changed processes, equipment upgrades and non-routine activities.
  Risk iden tification is undertaken by process owners in consultation with safety experts, with controls 
implemented in line with the hierarchy of controls. Departments set clear EHS objectives aligned to identified risks, supported by periodic reviews and continuous improvement. Insights from incidents, audits and operational experience are integrated into the risk assessment process to strengthen preventive controls and ensure regulatory compliance. This structured approach supports a safe, healthy and resilient workplace. Refer EHS Policy
Persistent Systems Limited  Annual Report 2026.

Business Responsibility and Sustainability ReportPRINCIPLE 4: Businesses should respect the interests of and be responsive to all its 
stakeholders
Essential Indicators
1. Describe the pr ocesses for identifying key stakeholder groups of the entity. 
  The Compan y follows a structured process to identify key stakeholder groups based on their relationship with the 
Company and relevance to its operations and value chain. Key stakeholder groups identified include employees, 
customers / partners, suppliers / vendors and business partners, investors and shareholders, government and regulators, and local communities. Stakeholder’s identification is undertaken using an impact–influence assessment, which considers both (a) the Company’s impact on stakeholders and (b) stakeholders’ ability to influence business outcomes. This process is integrated with the Company’s materiality assessment and risk management framework ensuring that stakeholder expectations and concerns are systematically evaluated and prioritised. As part of its governance framework, the Stakeholder’s Relationship and ESG Committee oversees stakeholder engagement through Management. The Committee regularly engages with stakeholders via multiple channels to assess key concerns, identify material topics, and evaluate their actual and potential impacts on the business. Inputs from these engagements are consolidated by Management and reviewed by the Committee as part of its ongoing oversight. The Stakeholders’ Relationship and ESG committee twice annually reviews stakeholder engagement initiatives at each meeting, assesses progress on material topics and refines engagement approaches to enhance effectiveness. Outcomes of these discussions are aligned with the Company’s broader ESG commitments and strategic priorities, ensuring transparency, ethical engagement, and sustained value creation for all stakeholders connected to the business. For more details refer “ESG Report FY 2025-26, Page 46”.

  Yes, Persistent Systems has a strong emphasis on accessibility and inclusion, with a focus on creating enablement 
friendly workplaces for persons with disabilities. The Company is committed to providing an inclusive, barrier free 
work environment and endeavours to ensure that its offices and premises are accessible in line with the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016, and the Harmonised Guidelines issued thereunder.

Renewable energy consumption for the reporting period comprises a combination of physical renewable

mix. In addition, the Company utilises International Renewable Energy Certificates (I -RECs) as market-based

Under the applied accounting methodology, Scope 2 emissions are disclosed using both location-based and market-based approaches in accordance with the GHG Protocol. -RECs are retired against grid electricity consumption to reflect 
contractual emission reductions. This dual approach ensures transparent reporting of renewable energy usage and supports the Company’s progress towards its decarbonisation and carbon neutrality objectives.

5.  Does the entity  have a business continuity and disaster management plan? Give details in 100 words / web link. 
Persistent Systems operates a mature, ISO/IEC 22301:2019–aligned Business Continuity Management System 
(BCMS) framework, integrated with ISO/IEC 27001 controls and embedded within Enterprise Risk Management. The framework spans all entities—subsidiaries, locations, functions and customer accounts—and is governed by defined roles with oversight from the Board’s Risk Management Committee and the CISO. BCM is driven by Business Impact Analysis and risk assessments, with resilience priorities aligned to financial materiality and contractual risk. Business Continuity Plans (BCPs) are implemented for critical services and key customer engagements, supported by industry-leading RTOs (up to 24 hours) and RPOs (up to 15 minutes). A multi-tiered approach, integrated with cyber resilience, crisis playbooks, and SOPs, ensures effective incident response. Robust Disaster Recovery (DR) testing, along with regular drills, simulations, and BC / DR exercises, is conducted to validate recovery capabilities and assure readiness. Periodic reviews and test outcomes drive continuous improvement and sustained operational resilience. Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery

  Implementa tion monitoring and progress tracking: The Project Manager, supported by the Delivery Excellence 
team, executes the CAPA plan. Implementation progress is monitored, reviewed periodically and updated within the PiQ system until completion.
  Resolution confirmation and formal closure: Upon resolution, the Delivery Partner secures customer 
acknowledgement of closure. The SQA team validates the effectiveness of actions taken and formally closes the escalation in PiQ, with relevant internal stakeholders kept informed.

Global Business Outlook
The global economy enters Financial Year 2025-26 against a backdrop of slowing growth and renewed inflationary 
pressure. These conditions are linked to last year’s trade barriers and elevated uncertainty, with ongoing conflict in the Middle East compounding the strain. The challenges are particularly acute for emerging markets and developing economies, which remain more vulnerable to external shocks and financial instability.
While increased defense spending in response to geopolitical tension may provide a temporary boost to economic 
activity, it also intensifies inflationary pressure and strains fiscal health, raising the likelihood of social unrest in fragile regions. The overall outlook remains clouded by substantial downside risks, including prolonged conflict, deepening geopolitical fragmentation and the resurgence of protectionist trade policies.
In this volatile environment, organisations are under pressure to strike a careful balance between cost efficiency 
and the need to build resilience, agility and progress toward climate objectives, especially as regulatory frameworks grow more complex and unpredictable. At the same time, rapid advances in automation and artificial intelligence are helping to reduce operational workloads, but these technologies require strong governance structures and proactive workforce reskilling to ensure successful integration. As your Company looks to 2026 and 2027, the pace of disruption is accelerating, with technology companies moving from experimental AI pilots to large-scale, ROI-focused deployments that prioritise safety, security and regulatory compliance, while also laying the groundwork for the adoption of transformative quantum technologies.
Company OutlookYour Company is a premier global provider of digital engineering and enterprise modernisation services. With more 
than 27,500 employees across 21 countries, it specialises in AI-driven solutions and software product engineering for industries such as BFSI, Healthcare and Hi-Tech, with deep expertise in building software products from conception to deployment. Its focus is on embedding AI-driven solutions across platforms, helping enterprises move from technical debt to competitive differentiation through a platform mindset.
Your company’s strategic approach centers on AI readiness through modern technology and data stacks, enabling 
clients to become value creators. It modernises core platforms and embeds AI across operations, aligning modernisation with strategic priorities to accelerate product launches, improve cost-to-income ratios and build customer trust. From product engineering to cloud and AI-powered automation, your Company drives smarter, safer and more sustainable industrial ecosystems. Its expertise in building next-generation software products at speed, with breakthrough operational efficiency, continues to be valued by its clients and its focus on delivering insights-driven, omnichannel customer experiences using best-in-class technologies underpins the long-term relationships it sustains with most of its customers.
Building the AI-led Enterprise For most enterprises, the question is no longer whether to adopt Generative AI, but where AI creates genuine value 
and where greater autonomy introduces risk. The market is shifting decisively from experimentation to disciplined, large-scale production. Generative AI is now firmly established from pilot to deployment, toward Agentic AI woven into core business processes. Yet realising AI’s full potential remains demanding. Integrating intelligence with  existing enterprise systems is both complex and expensive and outcomes must be governed, secure and dependable at scale.
Your Company’s AI strategy is anchored on three reinforcing pillars, underpinned by Responsible AI. Engineering 
Hyper-Productivity embeds AI across the software development lifecycle, so engineering teams deliver faster, raise quality and do more with less. Business Hyper-Productivity applies AI to automate and optimise business process workflows and decision-making across enterprise functions, enabling organisations to drive efficiency and faster outcomes. Enterprise Data Readiness prepares the enterprise data foundation, with the right structure, governance and accessibility so AI can deliver accurate, contextual and trusted outcomes at scale. Together, these pillars define the path enterprises must take to realise the full value of AI. Success lies in the last mile, making AI-driven outcomes repeatable, transparent and governed at scale, so that the desired business outcome is sustained and trusted across the enterprise.

The 3C Framework of Persistent AIUnderpinning these platforms and client engagements is your Company’s 3C Framework — Core, Context and 
Coordination — an architecture that moves AI from fragmented pilots to integrated, enterprise-wide outcomes,  and provides a repeatable path from experimentation to production at scale.

Context supplies the enterprise intelligence grounding agents in verified data, knowledge graphs, institutional

INR/$ Currency Movement
The Company minimises the foreign currency fluctuation risk as per the Company’s Foreign Exchange Risk 
Management Policy. The Company holds plain vanilla forward contracts against a portion of expected future receivables in USD to manage the risk of changes in exchange rates.
As per the accounting principles laid down in Ind AS 109 – ‘Financial Instruments’ relating to cash flow hedges, 
derivative financial instruments which qualify for cash flow hedge accounting are fair valued at balance sheet date and the effective portion of the resultant loss / (gain) is debited / (credited) to the hedge reserve under other comprehensive income and  the ineffective portion is recognised in the statement of profit and loss. Derivative financial instruments are carried as forward contract receivable when the fair value is positive and as forward contract payable when the fair value is negative.
Changes in the fair value of derivative instruments that do not qualify for hedge accounting are recognised in the 
statement of profit and loss as they arise. Hedge accounting is discontinued when the hedging instrument expires or is sold, or terminated, or exercised or no longer qualifies for hedge accounting. Any cumulative gain or loss on the hedging instrument recognised under other comprehensive income is transferred to the statement of profit and loss when the forecasted transaction occurs or affects profit or loss or when a hedged transaction is no longer expected to occur.
Accordingly, the Forward Cover Reserve (net of tax effects) as at March 31, 2026, stood at a debit balance of INR 
1,676.01 Million as against a debit balance of INR 2.32 Million as at March 31, 2025. Please refer to ‘Other Equity’ under Statement of Changes in Equity in the consolidated financials for details.
Exchange Differences on Translating the Financial Statements of Foreign OperationsWhile consolidating the financial statements of subsidiaries (including step down subsidiaries) with the financial 
statements of the Parent Company, the assets and liabilities are stated in Indian Rupees by applying the closing exchange rates, equity is stated in Indian Rupees by applying the historical exchange rates and income and expenditure are stated in Indian Rupees by applying the average exchange rates. This creates an exchange difference on consolidation, which is accumulated under the foreign currency translation reserve.
The balance in the foreign currency translation reserve was INR 3,358.33 Million as at March 31, 2026, as against 
INR 1,691.41 Million as at March 31, 2025. Please refer to ‘Other Equity’ under Statement of Changes in Equity in the consolidated financials for details.

Report on Risk Management
Persistent’s Approach to Risk Management 
Persistent has a robust Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework comprising a formal risk management policy, 
defined processes, governance mechanisms, and ongoing awareness programmes. Our ERM function is focused on strengthening and embedding a proactive risk management culture across the organisation. 
The ERM function works closely with various organisational units and business leadership to facilitate the identification, 
assessment, and management of risks. Oversight is provided by the Risk Management Committee (RMC) of the Board of Directors, which was constituted on April 24, 2017, ahead of the regulatory requirement for such a committee.
ERM Objectives
The key objectives of Persistent’s ERM function are to:
•  Promote an effective system to manage risks essential to support the Company’s growth strategy and business 
objectives, while ensuring resilience despite changing business dynamic
•  Impr ove institutional decision-making by providing senior management and the Board with timely and accurate 
information, and proposing mitigation plans, enabling them to better comprehend the risks and opportunities at the enterprise level and make informed decisions
•
  Ensur e that the Company meets all legal, regulatory, and policy compliance obligations
•  Establish a structured process to identify and assess risks that may impact the business continuity of the Company, 
and define appropriate response and recovery plans
•  Proactively identify potential risks and opportunities to prepare for future challenges and breakthroughs
•  Strengthen the organisation’s ability to comprehend, manage, and control risk exposures, fostering a culture of 
responsible risk -taking
•  Integrate risk and opportunity assessment into the Company’s periodic planning procedures, such as strategic 
planning and the annual budgeting cycle
•  Promote a Risk -Intelligent Culture wherein conscious, enterprise -wide efforts are made to align the organisation’s 
approach to risk, enabling consistent, risk-factored decision -making through targeted programmes such as Risk 
Familiarisation Programmes for Directors and Key Managerial Personnel, and risk training across key functions
ERM Framework
The Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework adopted by Persistent is aligned with ISO Standard 31000:2018 
Risk Management — Guidelines, COSO ERM — Integrating Strategy and Performance (2017), and applicable regulatory requirements in India. The framework takes a holistic approach to identifying the full range of risks the Company faces, with particular emphasis on those that are critical to strategic success. The framework provides guidance on identifying, assessing, measuring, monitoring, and responding to risks across the enterprise in alignment with the Company’s objectives and risk appetite. The ERM function reports enterprise
-level risks to executive 
leadership and the Risk Management Committee (RMC) of the Board on a timely basis as needed. A formal review is conducted quarterly.
The Company’s risk management framework is further strengthened through the active involvement of internal auditors 
and statutory auditors, who periodically review risk mitigation plans and related controls. Through their independent assessments and audit processes, they provide oversight of the Company’s risk management practices — reinforcing governance and supporting continuous improvement of enterprise risk management. The auditors also provide inputs on key risk areas and emerging concerns as part of the overall risk management process.
Responsibility for managing risks is shared across the organisation to ensure an effective and consistent process 
for avoiding and responding to risks in a timely manner. Dedicated leadership forums support the identification, monitoring, and tracking of enterprise
-level risks, while the Risk Management Committee (RMC) of the Board has 
ultimate oversight of the Company’s risk management function.
Report on Risk Management
358
=== page 279 ===
ERM Process Flow
The risk management process followed at Persistent comprises the following key steps:
• Risk Identifica tion: Identify plausible uncertainties and risks that may impact the achievement of functional, organisational, 
and business objectives, or pose a threat to business continuity. This includes risks arising from internal operations as well as 
external factors. Identified risks are categorised into financial, operational, reputational, regulatory, extended enterprise, strategic, sustainability, talent, and technology for further assessment.
•
 Risk Analy sis:
•  Existing and newly identified risks are analysed based on impact, likelihood, and velocity and are evaluated against 
established risk criteria, including potential business and financial impact
• For each enterprise -level risk, Key Risk Indicators (KRIs) are defined and monitored against approved risk appetite and 
tolerance thresholds to assess current risk health and the organisation’s readiness to manage it
• Wher e applicable, risks are assessed for potential financial exposure by identifying associated revenue, cost, or 
operational drivers. Probability of occurrence, inferred from KRI performance and risk assessment, is applied to estimate realistic downside impact and support prioritisation
•
 Selec ted risks are further analysed through scenario based assessments to evaluate the impact of plausible future 
conditions such as regulatory changes, market movements, or technological developments. Scenario outcomes help identify vulnerabilities and interdependencies, and inform mitigation planning
•
 Risk Prioritisa tion: Risks are prioritised based on criticality, emerging trends, and alignment with the Company’s objectives, 
enabling focused management attention on key risks
• Risk R esponse: Appropriate risk response strategies are defined to avoid, mitigate, or manage key enterprise-level risks. 
Mitigation plans are aligned to identified risk drivers, control effectiveness, and defined tolerance thresholds
•  Monit or and Review: Mitigation actions are integrated into day -to-day operations and monitored through defined indicators.  
The overall risk environment, effectiveness of mitigation measures, and emerging signals are reviewed periodically
•  Reporting: Consolidated risk insights, including risk status and key trends, are reported to executive leadership and the Risk Management Committee (RMC) of the Board on quarterly basis to support risk
-informed decision -making and oversight

Risk Categorisation
Risk categorisation at Persistent follows the ‘FORRESSSTT’ model, derived from the ‘PESTEL*’ model. Details of the 
FORRESSSTT model are as follows:
Risk Domains Definition
Financial Risk of potential financial loss resulting from breach of key risk indicators or ineffective or 
inefficient processes and controls
Operational Risk of potential breakdowns or deficiencies in process effectiveness or efficiency resulting from controls gaps or design weaknesses, which may cause material exposure
Reputational Risk of potential damage to reputation or loss of stakeholder confidence arising from non-compliance with risk management requirements, operational breakdown, legal or regulatory breach, unsuccessful product launches, or other adverse events
Regulatory Risk of potential fines, litigation costs, or enforcement actions from changes in the legal and regulatory environment, perceived or actual conflicts of interest, and potential actions or breaches of compliance and risk management requirements
Extended Enterprise Risk of potential disruption due to inadequate identification, assessment, or mitigation of 
risks associated with third
-party relationships
Sectoral Risks specific to the industry or sector in which the Company operates
Strategic Risks that could disrupt key assumptions underpinning the Company’s strategy, affecting strategic positioning, execution, or outcomes
Sustainability – ESG Risks associated with managing corporate responsibility and sustainable development issues 
that may impact long
-term growth and value creation for beneficiaries
Talent Risk arising from attrition, skill shortages, or workforce challenges relative to industry and market benchmarks
Technology & Cyber Risk arising from potential system failures, technology deficiencies, or unauthorised or 
malicious use of information systems
*PESTEL stands for Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal

Risk Governance Structure
The Company has established a governance structure based on three pillars of risk management responsibility:  
Risk Oversight, Risk Infrastructure and Management, and Risk Ownership. This structure cascades risk management responsibilities across senior management and all employees, including subsidiaries of the Company.
The risk management governance structure at Persistent is as follows:
Risk Governance 
and Oversight:
The Risk Governance 
and Oversight layer comprises the Board and Risk Management Committee, who will play a pivotal role in framing and approving the ERM Policy and guidelines for the organisation.
Risk Infrastructure and Management:
The Risk Infrastructure 
and Management layer comprises the Executive Risk Committee, ERM Function (CRO and ERM team) who shall support risk governance and oversight function and play a pivotal role in implementation  of ERM framework  in the company.
Risk Ownership:

layer comprises Risk Owners and various Risk committees who shall be responsible for performing risk management activities in the company.Board of

Audits
Enterprise-level resilience is continuously enhanced through rigorous audits and assessments conducted at both 
entity and functional levels. Key improvement opportunities identified through these reviews are incorporated by the respective teams into their processes and operations. Examples of audits and assessments conducted during the year include:
•
 Internal Audit of Organisational Units
• SOC- 2 Type 2 Audit
• Various ISO Audits
• Capability  Maturity Model Integration (CMMI) Assessments
Highlights of FY26FY2026 was marked by heightened geopolitical uncertainty and continued macro-economic volatility, including 
regional geopolitical developments, global trade and tariff-related uncertainty, and policy-led industry considerations. Throughout the year, the Company closely monitored these developments and activated appropriate mitigation measures to safeguard business continuity, workforce safety, and customer delivery. The Company’s diversified delivery footprint, established business continuity planning, and crisis management arrangements enabled stable operations during the period. These developments did not have a material impact on the Company’s operations, financial performance, or delivery commitments during FY 2026. However, given the evolving nature of the external risk environment, these areas remain under active monitoring and are supported by scenario-based contingency planning. 
Geopolitical and macro-economic developments were assessed through structured enterprise-level risk reviews and 
ongoing management oversight. The Company’s service-oriented business model, geographic diversification, and limited exposure to high-risk regions supported operational resilience. Proactive stakeholder communication and operational flexibility further enabled continuity during the year. 
Against this backdrop, the Company continued to strengthen its enterprise risk management framework with a 
forward-looking focus. Increased emphasis was placed on emerging and evolving risks, including artificial intelligence-related considerations, cyber security and data privacy, regulatory and labour-law developments, and macro-economic uncertainty. These risks were addressed through structured assessments, enhanced control frameworks, employee awareness initiatives, and scenario-based resilience testing to support informed decision-making.
Risk governance and crisis preparedness capabilities were further enhanced during the year. An integrated risk 
intelligence platform supported consolidated risk visibility, key risk indicator monitoring, and timely escalation to senior management and the Board Risk Committee. Ongoing regulatory monitoring, materiality reassessment, and strengthened governance practices reinforced the Company’s ability to anticipate and respond effectively to changes in the external risk environment.
The Company believes that the continued strengthening of risk governance, resilience, and forward-looking risk 
assessment capabilities remains critical to sustaining long-term growth and maintaining stakeholder confidence.

To the Members of Persistent Systems Limited
Report on the Audit of the Consolidated Financial Statements OpinionWe have audited the consolidated financial statements of Persistent Systems Limited (hereinafter referred to as the 
“Holding Company”) and its subsidiaries (Holding Company and its subsidiaries together referred to as “the Group”) and its Employee Stock Option Plan Trust (“ESOP trust”), which comprise the consolidated balance sheet as at 31 March 2026, and the consolidated statement of profit and loss (including other comprehensive income), consolidated statement of changes in equity and consolidated statement of cash flows for the year then ended, and notes to the consolidated financial statements, including material accounting policies and other explanatory information (hereinafter referred to as “the consolidated financial statements”).
In our opinion and to the best of our information and according to the explanations given to us, and based on the 
consideration of report of the other auditor on separate financial statements of such subsidiary as were audited by the other auditor, the aforesaid consolidated financial statements give the information required by the Companies Act, 2013 (“Act”) in the manner so required and give a true and fair view in conformity with the accounting principles generally accepted in India, of the consolidated state of affairs of the Group as at 31 March 2026, of its consolidated profit and other comprehensive income, consolidated changes in equity and consolidated cash flows for the year then ended.
Basis for OpinionWe conducted our audit in accordance with the Standards on Auditing (SAs) specified under Section 143(10) of the

We are independent of the Group in accordance with the ethical requirements that are relevant to our audit of the consolidated financial statements in terms of the Code of Ethics issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and the relevant provisions of the Act, and we have fulfilled our other ethical responsibilities in accordance with these requirements. === page 297 ===
Revenue recognition on fixed price contracts, wherein revenue is recognised using percentage 
of completion method
See Note 25 to consolidated financial statementsThe key audit matter How the matter was addressed in our audit
The Group inter alia engages in Fixed-price contracts, 
wherein, revenue is recognised over the period of time using the percentage of completion computed as per the input method. This is based on the Group’s estimate of efforts to complete the contracts.
Revenue recognition of fixed price contracts where the 
percentage of completion is used is identified as a key audit matter since —
•
 there is an inherent risk and presumed fraud risk 
around the existence of revenue recognised 
considering the customised and complex nature of these contracts;
•
 applica tion of revenue recognition using percentage 
of completion under accounting standard (Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with customers) is complex and involves:
     i.  
 estimating the future effort-to complete these 
contracts, which is used to measure the stage of completion of the relevant performance obligation; and
    ii.  
 judgemen t in identification of distinct performance 
obligations and determination of transaction price for such performance obligations.
•
 further , these contracts may involve onerous 
obligations which requires critical assessment of foreseeable losses to be made by the Group; and
•
 at year-end, significant amount of contract assets 
and; unearned revenue balances related to these contracts are recognised on the balance sheet.In view of the significance of the matter, we applied the following audit procedures in this area, among others to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence:
•
 Obtained an under standing of the systems, processes 
and controls for determining and recording revenue 
and the associated contract assets and unearned revenue balances.
•
 Evaluated the design and tested the operating 
effectiveness of management’s key internal controls (including key IT controls) over revenue recognition.
•
 On a selec tion of contracts, we tested if the revenue 
recognised was in accordance with the revenue recognition accounting standard.
•
 We:
     i.   evaluated the identification of performance 
obligations;
     ii.   consider ed the terms of the contracts to determine 
the transaction price;
   iii.   determined if the Group’s evaluation of the method 
used for recognition of revenue is appropriate;
   iv.   assessed if  the estimates of efforts to complete were 
reviewed and approved by appropriate designated management personnel;
   v.  
 tested the Group’s calculation of efforts incurred 
till date and estimation of efforts to complete the contract including estimation of onerous obligations, if any,

Impairment of Goodwill
See Note 5.4 to consolidated financial statementsThe key audit matter How the matter was addressed in our audit
The Group is required to test goodwill for 
impairment every year or more frequently when there is an indication of impairment. The impairment charge is determined by comparing the carrying value of goodwill with its recoverable amount. Recoverable amount is defined as the higher of value in use and fair value less cost of disposal. We consider the impairment testing of goodwill by the Group allocated to Cloud, Infrastructure and Security (CIS) and Customer Experience (CXCI) Cash Generating Units (CGUs) to involve significant estimates and judgment with a potential range of reasonable outcomes greater than our materiality for the consolidated financial statements as a whole.
There is inherent uncertainty involved in 
forecasting and discounting future cashflows, which are the basis of the assessment of recoverability. Considering the significant judgement involved, impairment of goodwill allocated to above mentioned CGUs are identified as key audit matter.In view of the significance of the matter we applied the following audit procedures in this area, among others to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence:
•
 Obtained an under standing of Group’s evaluation of 
identification of cash generating units and allocation of 
goodwill to the respective CGUs. 
• Obtained managemen t’s assessment of recoverable amount 
and impairment assessment for goodwill.
• Tested the design, implementation and operating 
effectiveness of controls in respect of the Group’s impairment assessment process, including the periodic review of cashflow forecasts and valuation assumptions.
•
 Wher e management has used an independent valuer, 
evaluated the independent valuer’s competence, capabilities and objectivity, and assessing the valuation methodology used by the independent valuer to estimate the value in use.
•
 Evaluated the reasonableness of the cash flow projections 
and assessed the underlying key assumptions like revenue growth rate, projected margins, discount rates and terminal growth rate used in management’s valuation working to determine recoverable amount by considering recent financial performance and externally derived data.
•
 Engaged independen t valuation specialists to assist in the 
evaluation of assumptions and methodologies used by the Group and its experts.
•
 Assessed the impac t of sensitivity over assumptions used by 
the management in determining the value in use.
• Assessed the appr opriateness of the related disclosures in 
the consolidated financial statements.

Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements
A company’s internal financial controls with reference to financial statements is a process designed to provide 
reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company’s internal financial controls with reference to financial statements include those policies and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company; (2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorisations of management and directors of the company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, use, or disposition of the company’s assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements.
Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial StatementsBecause of the inherent limitations of internal financial controls with reference to financial statements, including the 
possibility of collusion or improper management override of controls, material misstatements due to error or fraud may occur and not be detected. Also, projections of any evaluation of the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements to future periods are subject to the risk that the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate.
Other MatterOur aforesaid report under Section 143(3)(i) of the Act on the adequacy and operating effectiveness of the internal 
financial controls with reference to financial statements insofar as it relates to two subsidiary companies, which are companies incorporated in India, is based on the corresponding reports of the auditors of such companies incorporated in India.

Nature and purpose of reserves
a)  General reserve
  The gener al reserve is a free reserve created by an appropriation from one component of equity (generally 
retained earnings) to another, not being an item of other comprehensive income (“OCI”). The same can be utilised 
in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
b)  Shar e options outstanding reserve
  Shar e options outstanding reserve represents the cumulative expense recognised for equity-settled transactions 
at each reporting date until the employee share options are exercised / expired upon which such amount is transferred to General reserve. 
c)
  Capital reserve
  The e xcess of the Group’s portion of equity of the acquired company over its cost is treated as gain on bargain 
purchase and disclosed under Capital Reserve in the financial statements. 
d)  Capital r edemption reserve
  Capital r edemption reserve represents the nominal value of the shares bought back; and is created and utilised in 
accordance with section 69 of the Companies Act, 2013.
e)  Cash flo w hedge reserve
  When a deriv ative is designated as cashflow hedging instrument, the effective portion of changes in the fair value 
of derivative is recognised in other comprehensive income (OCI) and accumulated in cashflow hedge reserve. Cumulative gains or losses previously recognised in cashflow hedge reserve are recognised in the statement of profit and loss in the period in which such transaction occurs / hedging instruments are settled / cancelled.
f)
  Foreign currency translation reserve
  The f oreign exchange differences arising from the translation of financial statements of foreign operations with 
functional currency other than Indian rupees is recognised in other comprehensive income and is presented under equity in the foreign currency translation reserve. The amount is transferred to retained earnings upon disposal of investment in foreign operation.
g)
  PSPL  ESOP Trust reserve and Treasury shares
  The Gr oup has created an Employee Stock Options Trust (ESOP Trust) for providing share-based payment to its 
employees. The Group uses ESOP Trust as a vehicle for distributing shares to employees. The ESOP Trust buys shares of the Company from the market, for giving shares to employees. The shares held by ESOP Trust are treated as treasury shares. Own equity instruments that are reacquired (treasury shares) are recognised at cost and deducted from equity. No gain or loss is recognised in profit or loss on the purchase, sale, issue or cancellation of the Group’s own equity instruments. Any difference between the carrying amount and the consideration, if reissued, is recognised in equity. Share options whenever exercised, would be satisfied with treasury shares.
h)
  Securities premium
  Securities pr emium is used to record the premium on issue of shares. The reserve is utilised in accordance with the 
provisions of section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013.
i)  Retained earnings
  Retained earnings represent the amount of accumulated earnings of the Group which includes remeasurements of 
the defined benefit liabilities / asset.Consolidated Financials

1. Gr oup Overview
Persistent Systems Limited (“the Parent Company” or “PSL”) is a public company domiciled in India and 
incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 (“the 1956 Act”). The Company has its registered office at Bhageerath, 402 Senapati Bapat Road, Pune, Maharashtra, India. The shares of PSL are listed on Bombay Stock Exchange and National Stock Exchange. PSL is a global company specialising in software products, services and technology innovation. PSL together with its subsidiaries and controlled trust, is hereinafter referred to as ‘the Group’. The Group offers complete product life cycle services.
The Board of Directors approved the consolidated financial statements for the year ended March 31, 2026 and 
authorised for issue on April 21, 2026.
